items.title: Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5
items.content:
Update on GitHub

Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.

With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?

I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.

Two goals

I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.

For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.

How it works

The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:

[
  {"name": "dream", "prompt": "Style: cinematic, realistic, shallow depth of field. A plump seal ... is fast asleep on warm golden sand under palm trees ...",
   "seed": 3},
  {"name": "nap", "prompt": "Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... a plump grey seal is fast asleep on a small ice floe ...",
   "seed": 1, "to": {"shot": "iceberg", "frames": 9}},
  {"name": "iceberg", "prompt": "Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... the whole iceberg slowly rolls over ... and washes over the seal. ..."},
  {"name": "shake", "prompt": "Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... It slowly shakes its head and body ... and flops down on its belly on the floe, ...",
   "from": {"shot": "iceberg", "frames": 25}}
]

Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:

  • from: the shot starts from the last frames of an earlier shot. Starting from the earlier shot's last frame keeps a subject's look across a cut; starting from its last 25 frames (1 s) also continues the motion.
  • to: the shot ends on the first frames of a later shot, so that it leads into it.

A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.

Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg.

The payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest.

On the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5. LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps.

The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. The film part is about 160 lines of Python on top: read the film file, order the shots so each keyframe exists before the shot that needs it, and cut the frames to hand over; then trim, caption, even out the sound and assemble the film. The code is in dacorvo/video-generation. The films I kept are in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket, with their JSON files: the seal, the fox, and the goat, which trims two of its shots and draws a caption over its payoff.

Running on Trainium3

Out of the box, the model does not run on the NeuronCores: the transformer does not fit on one, and diffusers has no plan to split it. The first attempt that ran (the model card's pipeline, with the transformer split over 4 cores and a few patches) took about 5 min 20 s for a 10-second clip, and the NeuronCores were actually computing for only about 45 s of it. What's more, the target resolution was out of reach.

Five days later:

10-second clip with sound NeuronCores Wall time On the NeuronCores vs. first attempt
First attempt, 960×544 4 5 min 20 s 45 s 1×
Optimized, 2048×1024 (~4× more pixels) 32 22 to 23 s 15 s 14×

Getting there took three kinds of work: making the model run on the NeuronCores (requires tensor parallelism), splitting it over more of them (sequence parallelism), and making the host keep up with them.

Most of the fixes below are on the device, and that is where most of the effort went. The biggest end-to-end savings came from the host: the low-hanging fruit, since that is obviously where the waste was.

What it took to make it work

Problem Workaround Result
The transformer does not fit on one NeuronCore, and diffusers has no tensor-parallel plan for it A plan, and an attention processor that runs on the heads of one rank The transformer runs on 4 cores
The text encoder does not fit on a NeuronCore next to the transformer, so it runs on the CPUs. diffusers supports a pipeline split this way, but its LTX-2 pipelines give the text encoder its inputs on the NeuronCores Pin the pipeline to the host, and move the transformer's inputs to the cores and its outputs back The pipeline runs with its transformer on the cores
Compiled as one graph, the transformer returned NaN at one size, and each new process traced it again, even with every graph in the cache Compile one block with compile_repeated_blocks Finite outputs, and tracing falls from 388 s to 18 s
torch-neuronx computes a bf16 GELU entirely in bf16, constants included (#1049) Compute the GELUs in fp32 Transformer error against fp32: 0.297 → 0.158 (CPU bf16: 0.160)
At 2048×1024, the block graph of the transformer split 4 ways fails to load Split the video tokens 8 ways on top (sequence parallelism): two custom attention processors on diffusers' set_attn_processor hook, each a few tensor reshapes around its collective calls (code) Stage 2 runs on 4 × 8 = 32 cores, at 3.0 s a step
A shot that starts from frames has a timestep per video token, and its block graph fails to load Embed only the two timesteps, and pick one for each token (code) A shot from frames takes about as long as one from a prompt

What it took to make it fast

Problem Workaround Gain
Each rank (one process per NeuronCore) ran the whole pipeline, and they all encoded the prompt on the CPUs of one socket Run the pipeline on rank 0 only, and send the other ranks the arguments of each call Prompt encoding: about 205 s → 7.5 s
torch-neuronx's allocator leaves most of its memory segments unused (#1052) Pack the parameters into buffers of at most 1 GiB Memory per core: 22.96 GiB → 10.2 GiB
The attention runs as plain ops unless the sequence length is a multiple of 128 tokens Generate at 1024×512 (512 tokens per frame), with NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 Transformer step: 4.3 s → 3.0 s
The video decode is slow on CPU, and more CPU cores do not help Decode on the NeuronCores, split by frames, and pass the frames to rank 0 through shared memory Decode at 2048×1024: 357 s → 1.6 s
A strided slice copied to the device is filled by a slow copy on the device (#1050) .contiguous() before the copy Step on 16 cores: 5.6 s → 1.0 s
Rank 0 alone runs the pipeline's CPU stages (text encoder, upsampler, vocoder), but every rank gets a node-wide torch thread pool, and 31 ranks starve it Pin rank 0's threads to the CPUs no other rank uses, and cap the other ranks' threads to their fair share (code) Prompt encoding: 7.4 s → 3.3 s. Stage 1 step: 0.9 s → 0.6 s
The pipeline pads the prompt to 1024 tokens, and the text encoder, on CPU, encodes the padding too Run the text encoder on the tokens of the prompt only Prompt encoding: 3.4 s → 1.4 s

Three issues were never explained: the transformer compiled as one graph returned NaN at one size, the first shot that ends on keyframes was slow in each new process (even with every graph in the cache), and the latent upsampler fails to load next to the transformer, so it stays on the CPU.

Some of this is being fixed upstream. diffusers#15420 (open) fixes the LTX-2 pipelines, which would make the second workaround above unnecessary. diffusers#14725 (still open) brings tensor and context parallelism into one ParallelConfig, and a _tp_plan for LTX-2.5 is planned.

Lessons learned

  • Both sides fell hard: the host and the device. Once running, a clip's host time fell from about 280 s to about 8 s (~35×), and its time on the NeuronCores from 45 s to 15 s (3×, at four times the pixels, and with a second stage the first attempt could not even load).
  • Sequence parallelism is how one clip uses the machine. Tensor parallelism is imposed by memory (the transformer does not fit on one core) and capped by the 32 attention heads. Splitting the sequence over more cores is what puts 32 of the 64 NeuronCores on a single clip, and what made 2048×1024 possible at all, by shrinking each core's graph until it loaded.
  • On Trainium, plan for the size of the graphs. The shapes decide whether the attention takes the fast kernel, and graphs that are too large fail to load.
  • Check against the CPU first. Each split of the models was checked on CPU before it ran on the device, and the comparison with CPU found the GELU issue.
  • Keep the traced code stable. In the build I used, torch-neuronx's cache key included the file and line of each traced op, so an edit could trigger a recompile of up to 30 minutes per graph. I had already reported it (aws-neuron/torch-neuronx#1027), and the issue is now closed.
  • A film needs more than prompts. Prompts alone do not keep a character, or a mountain, from one shot to the next, so shots start or end on frames of other shots. Each shot also stays in one place: when a shot in an early version of the fox film took the fox from the forest to the lake, the model made a cross-dissolve to another fox.
  • Make several takes of each shot. The model often gets a detail wrong: the same prompt gave the goat funny horns in 3 takes out of 4. I made 4 takes of each new shot and picked one.

Professional use cases

On the performance side, once the models are loaded, a 10-second 2048×1024 clip with sound takes 22 to 23 s. That rivals LTX's paid API, on half of the instance. A service would keep its processes up, as they take about 3 minutes to load the models, and 80 s for their first clip.

On the feature side, diffusers has what it takes to draft a movie. The shots come from prompts, and keep their subject from one shot to the next by starting or ending on frames of other shots. Takes differ by their seed, and the film file keeps the one I picked. Re-run with the same code and film file, and you get the same film back, byte for byte. A shot can also start from an image, such as a storyboard frame or a character sheet, which the condition pipeline takes the same way as frames (I did not try it in a film).

What keeps it at drafts:

  • The model still gets details wrong, so each new shot needs several takes.
  • Each shot makes its own sound. The film evens out the background level, but the sound does not carry over from one shot to the next.
  • A shot lasts at most 20 s, the model's limit.

From films to world models

LTX calls LTX-2.5 a world model, with robotics as an emerging use. Robots, cars and drones learn from videos of what their cameras see, and a world model can make more of them, including events too rare or too risky to film. So I also tried it on real footage, with the same code: a shot can start from the first second of a real camera clip and invent what happens next. One frame was not enough, as the model cannot tell from it how fast things move.

Here is the head camera of a Fourier GR1-T2 humanoid robot (a clip from NVIDIA's GR1-100), looking down at a table. In the real 6-second clip, the robot's left hand picks an orange from a plate and drops it in a tray. The model only sees the first second of that clip (the hands raised, before anything moves) and invents the rest. What really happened, next to its invention:

Same scene, same pick: the model invents the grab on its own, and keeps the table, the hands and the fruit consistent with the real footage. More interesting are the events that did not happen. From the same second, with only the prompt changed, a person leans over and grabs the orange too, and the human hand and the robot hand carry it to the tray together. Five takes, with the real footage first:

The person's gestures and timing differ in each take, and the robot's arm adapts to them. That is the appeal for training: not one continuation of a clip, but a distribution of them, each reproducible from its film file and seed.

The robotics folder of the bucket has the five takes with their JSON files, and a second example from the front camera of a car in a snowstorm (Boreas), where the alternate event is slush thrown on the lens by a passing truck. Asked to make the car accelerate instead, the model kept its speed: the prompt does not override what the first second of footage already implies.

These videos follow prompts, not the robot's or car's commands: a training setup would need generation conditioned on those actions. For that, a team fine-tunes the pre-trained checkpoint of LTX-2.5 on the frames and actions of its own robots.

The Ferrari made it around the track, on half of its cylinders.

items.title: Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon
items.content:
The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

Quick start

You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

  1. In the Overview tab, compare quantizations for one hardware, model, and build. The two charts show PP512 (512 input tokens, no generation) and TG128 (128 generated tokens), both starting at context depth zero.
  2. In the Build history tab, track PP512 and TG128 across all recorded builds for the selected hardware, model, and quantization.
  3. In the Context scaling tab, see how token-generation throughput changes as the existing context grows, for the selected build, hardware, model, and quantization.

What the numbers mean

The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:

Test Workload What it helps you assess
PP512 Process 512 input tokens How quickly the model processes a prompt
TG128 Generate 128 tokens How quickly the model produces output

Both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

How we run the benchmarks

We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

Inspect and reuse the results

The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

Standard results use <build>/<hardware>/<model>/<quant>.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder <quant>-tg.jsonl filename.

Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.

Join the conversation

Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard, inspect the data, and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

items.title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference
items.content:
We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

What Parse 3.5 produces

Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation.

This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training:

  • Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.

  • Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.

  • OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language.

Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry

SFT teaches the capability; RLVR improves consistency

We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents.

We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content.

A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output.

Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods.

The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts.

Faster inference through architecture and DFlash2

A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs.

Component Parse 2.0 Parse 3.5
Page preprocessing Fixed 2048 × 1664 canvas NaViT dynamic rectangular inputs
Image-to-text connection Encoder–decoder cross-attention Compressed visual tokens as a causal prefix
Decoder self-attention Multi-head attention GQA-8: 16 query heads, 8 key/value heads
Speculative decoding One-token lookahead (MTP); optional DFlash2

NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory.

The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token.

Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details.

In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively.

Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it:

  1. Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts.

  2. Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output.

  3. Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass

Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests.

In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements.

Apply the same SFT/RLVR approach to your documents

We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, and NeMo RL GRPO, using vLLM to generate candidate answers.

The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram: a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth.

Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label.

RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR.

Figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol.

To adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output.

We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models.

We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review.

items.title: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems
items.content:
Update on GitHub

Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate

This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models.

That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50.

Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents?

In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from.

First, we'll start off with some context on swarms.

The rise of the swarms

We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem.

But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so.

When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same.

Did cooperation help, or did we just spend more?

Start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries.

Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided.

This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute?

We understand that question through this simple expectation.

We'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms.

A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture.

A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training.

A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward.

Agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are:

  • A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog.

  • A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL.

Our first experiment: four agents ordering numbers

We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows.

Each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is:

#### [5, 5, 26, 78]

The team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list. One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates.

This means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful.

The main communication tools are message(to, text), read_messages(), and check_notifications(). A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone.

We defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy, with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments.

A team reward and eight attempts at each problem

In this post, a team means one episode: four agents attempting one problem once. A successful team receives a reward reduced by the tokens it uses. A failed team receives zero:

team allowance = 4 × (8,192 work tokens + 1,024 final-answer tokens)
               = 36,864 tokens

reward = success × (1 − 0.25 × min(1, generated team tokens / 36,864))

For illustration, a correct team using half its allowance receives 0.875. There is no separate reward for sending messages. The incentive is to solve the task while using fewer generated tokens.

For every training problem, we collect eight independent team attempts. Their rewards are normalized within that group. An attempt that does better than its group average gets a positive advantage; one that does worse gets a negative advantage. Every agent in the same team receives that team's advantage, including an agent whose own final answer was wrong.

In TRL, each agent's sampled tokens form a training row. Its incoming messages and tool results provide context. The loss is averaged within each team and then across teams, so longer conversations do not give a team more weight.

Our results come from the original experiment, which used 256 team attempts per update (32 problems with eight attempts each). The walkthrough uses TRL's default of --teams-per-update 128, which works out to about 150 team attempts per update.

Our Results

Over 75 steps, training success rose from 6.6% to 82.3%, comparing the first and last five updates. At checkpoint 75, the four-agent team solved 26 of 32 held-out problems (81.25%). The paper reports 93.2% four-agent success after 200 updates.

The team also used 37.4% fewer tokens per attempt, falling from about 13k to 8k. This improvement accompanied more active information sharing: broadcasts increased from 2.38 to 5.73 per team, even as total token use fell.

The team also used fewer tokens later in training. Comparing the first five updates with updates 71–75:

Training metric Updates 1–5, mean Updates 71–75, mean
Success 6.56% 82.34%
Generated tokens per team 12,826.9 8,026.0
Messages per team 3.48 6.28
Broadcasts per team 2.38 5.73
Teams with one broadcast per agent 4.06% 18.20%

That is a 37.4% reduction in generated tokens per training team between those windows. At batch 75 itself, the mean was 7,624 tokens per team. These are training measurements; we did not retain held-out token-efficiency measurements for the trained checkpoint.

Notice that fewer tokens did not mean fewer messages. More agents began participating but broadcasting became more common, rather than direct messaging. Generated tokens include reasoning and tool calls as well as message bodies, so message count alone does not tell us how much text the team produced.

No agent can solve the problem alone, so the closest equivalent of "a single agent with more retries" is the untrained team with more retries. The training data already contains this comparison. Each update collects eight attempts per problem, and the task's answers are easy to check, so we can count a problem as solved when any of its eight attempts succeeded. Early in training, that count gives the untrained team's best-of-8 success rate:

Success Generated tokens per problem
Untrained team, best of 8 attempts (updates 1–5) 37.5% about 103,000
Trained team, one attempt (updates 71–75) 82.3% about 8,000

With eight retries, the untrained team solves fewer than half the problems and spends about 13 times as many tokens as one attempt from the trained team. Read this as an estimate. Both rows use training problems rather than held-out ones, and updates 2–5 already sample from a slightly trained policy.

The model is small, but the rollouts are not. Each update generates millions of tokens of agent conversation at contexts of up to 40k tokens. We used one H200 for the trainer and seven H200s running vLLM rollout engines to get through those rollouts quickly, and kept each worker's eight attempts together. The walkthrough below runs the same task on two GPUs. Here are the infra details:

Setting Recorded experiment
Shared policy Qwen3-0.6B
Logical agents per team 4
Problems per update 32
Team attempts per problem 8
Work / final tokens per agent 8,192 / 1,024
Learning rate / temperature 5e-7 / 1.0
Training problem pool 1,024 generated problems
Reporting endpoint Preserved checkpoint 75
Execution 1 trainer GPU + 7 rollout GPUs

Practical example: Train your own swarm

The figures above describe our original 75-update experiment. In this walkthrough we'll run TRL's swarm example on Hugging Face Jobs. One H200 serves the shared Qwen3-0.6B policy with vLLM and a second H200 trains it.

1. Create a bucket for the run

Sign in with a Hugging Face account that can run Jobs and create buckets. Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your Hub username.

Use a fresh bucket for each run so earlier measurements stay available.

uv tool install 'huggingface_hub==2.4.0'
hf auth login
BUCKET="YOUR_USERNAME/swarm-trl-$(date -u +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
hf buckets create "$BUCKET"

2. Run the TRL example on Hugging Face Jobs

Save the script below as train-swarm.sh in your current directory.

train-swarm.sh 
set -eu
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/huggingface/trl /tmp/trl
cd /tmp/trl
example=examples/async_grpo_s3_aggregation
if [ ! -f "$example/async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py" ]; then
  git fetch --depth 1 origin refs/pull/8424/head
  git checkout --detach FETCH_HEAD
fi
git rev-parse HEAD > /results/trl-revision.txt
python -m pip install -e ".[vllm,kernels]" "vllm==0.32.0" datasets httpx trackio

base=Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B
url=http://127.0.0.1:8000
export TRACKIO_DIR=/tmp/trackio
serve() {
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1 vllm serve "$@" \
    --host 127.0.0.1 --max-model-len 40960 --max-num-seqs 512 --enable-prefix-caching &
  server=$!
  until curl -fs "$url/health" >/dev/null; do kill -0 "$server"; sleep 5; done
}
evaluate() {
  python "$example/evaluate.py" --url "$url" --model "$1" --name "$2" \
    --episodes 192 --concurrency 64 --out "/results/$2.jsonl"
}

serve "$base" --logprobs-mode processed_logprobs --weight-transfer-config "{\"backend\":\"nccl\"}"
evaluate "$base" base
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 accelerate launch --num_processes 1 --mixed_precision bf16 \
  "$example/async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py" --vllm-url "$url" \
  --updates 50 --teams-per-update 128 --concurrent-teams 128 \
  --report-to trackio --output-dir /tmp/swarm
cp -r "$TRACKIO_DIR" /tmp/swarm/checkpoint-50 /results/
kill "$server"
wait "$server" || true
serve /tmp/swarm/checkpoint-50 --logprobs-mode processed_logprobs
evaluate /tmp/swarm/checkpoint-50 trained

The command below sends its contents to the job. Inside the job, vLLM serves the shared policy on GPU 0. GPU 1 runs TRL's async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py for 50 updates with Trackio. TRL's evaluate.py scores the base model and checkpoint 50 on the same 192 held-out problems. That is a larger set than the 32-problem checks in our results, which gives tighter error bars. The job saves both scores, the checkpoint, Trackio data and the exact Git commit to your bucket.

  --volume "hf://buckets/$BUCKET:/results" \
  -- vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0 bash -c "$(cat train-swarm.sh)"

Each update uses about 150 team attempts. TRL packs micro-batches by token count rather than by team, so the --teams-per-update 128 setting is approximate. The --report-to trackio flag records training metrics at every update.

Each line of base.jsonl or trained.jsonl records one of those evaluation attempts.

hf buckets sync "hf://buckets/$BUCKET" ./swarm-results
TRACKIO_DIR="$PWD/swarm-results/trackio" uvx trackio show

This first example gives us a small environment, a shared reward and a policy that improves at pooling private information. It also shows why success, token use and communication structure need to be read together. At 75 updates, the team is solving most checked problems, but it has not converged to the cleanest communication pattern.

In the coming examples, we'll take a step back from training and look at how we evaluate and analyze swarms.

For now, we have something concrete to build on: four small agents, one trainable policy, a checkable task, and a reproducible way to examine what the team learned.

Each line of base.jsonl or trained.jsonl records one of those evaluation attempts.
hf buckets sync "hf://buckets/$BUCKET" ./swarm-results
TRACKIO_DIR="$PWD/swarm-results/trackio" uvx trackio show





What we'll try next


This first example gives us a small environment, a shared reward and a policy that improves at pooling private information. It also shows why success, token use and communication structure need to be read together. At 75 updates, the team is solving most checked problems, but it has not converged to the cleanest communication pattern.
In the coming examples, we'll take a step back from training and look at how we evaluate and analyze swarms.
For now, we have something concrete to build on: four small agents, one trainable policy, a checkable task, and a reproducible way to examine what the team learned.

items.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
items.content:
📄 Tech Report

Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.

Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

Helping researchers check the work

For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

Keep scientific judgment in the loop

Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”

Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said.

Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

The same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Meanwhile, participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used.

Both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

This is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

Build AI agents alongside scientists

Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

Researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

It will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify important concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

Still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

The promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

items.title: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
items.content:
Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

The use case: a Farm Assistant

A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:

  1. Listens and turns the speech into text.
  2. Searches a 154-page agricultural handbook, which is written in English.
  3. Answers in two to four spoken sentences, in the language the question was asked in, using only what the handbook says.
  4. Speaks the answer back and shows the source pages, so the answer can be checked.

If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

Where CUGA fits

CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:

  • One agent, any model. Switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting.
  • The knowledge engine. Parse a PDF, chunk it, embed it, and search it locally with agent.knowledge.search().
  • Conversation threads. Each question gets a fresh thread, so one person's language or context never leaks into another's.

The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio

Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

The hard part is not the voice

Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

Making it sound right and keeping it safe

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:

  • Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech.
  • Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC, and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast.
  • Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user.
  • Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key.

Try it

You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:

CUGA Apps on Hugging Face →

Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

Beyond farming: Scaling for Bharat

Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

Learn more about CUGA

New to CUGA? Here are some places to start:

  • cuga.dev: the CUGA home page.
  • CUGA on GitHub: the open-source harness (Apache 2.0). Star it, file issues, or pick up a good first issue.
  • CUGA documentation: setup, the SDK, knowledge, policies and configuration.
  • CUGA Apps gallery on GitHub: the source for the apps in the Hugging Face Space.

Spaces you can try in your browser:

  • CUGA Agent: the general-purpose agent, running on a demo CRM scenario.
  • CUGA Apps: launch working CUGA apps from one dashboard.
  • CUGA Policy Playground: two live agents side by side, one with policies and one without.

More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog:

  • CUGA on Hugging Face: Democratizing Configurable AI Agents: the introduction to CUGA and its configurable reasoning modes.
  • Build real agentic apps using CUGA: two dozen working examples on a lightweight harness: the app gallery this voice agent belongs to.
  • Same Model, Different Harness: CUGA, Hermes, and Deep Agents — When to Pick CUGA?: how much the harness matters when the model stays the same.

We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.




The hard part is not the voice


Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.
Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.
The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.
Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.




Making it sound right and keeping it safe


A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:
Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech.
Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC, and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast.
Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user.
Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key.




Try it


You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:
CUGA Apps on Hugging Face →
Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.




Beyond farming: Scaling for Bharat


Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.
Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.
This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.
If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.




Learn more about CUGA


New to CUGA? Here are some places to start:
cuga.dev: the CUGA home page.
CUGA on GitHub: the open-source harness (Apache 2.0). Star it, file issues, or pick up a good first issue.
CUGA documentation: setup, the SDK, knowledge, policies and configuration.
CUGA Apps gallery on GitHub: the source for the apps in the Hugging Face Space.
Spaces you can try in your browser:
CUGA Agent: the general-purpose agent, running on a demo CRM scenario.
CUGA Apps: launch working CUGA apps from one dashboard.
CUGA Policy Playground: two live agents side by side, one with policies and one without.
More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog:
CUGA on Hugging Face: Democratizing Configurable AI Agents: the introduction to CUGA and its configurable reasoning modes.
Build real agentic apps using CUGA: two dozen working examples on a lightweight harness: the app gallery this voice agent belongs to.
Same Model, Different Harness: CUGA, Hermes, and Deep Agents — When to Pick CUGA?: how much the harness matters when the model stays the same.

items.title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
items.content:
Update on GitHub

Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here.

One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs (sm100), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ.

We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint. Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs, and let it run experiments for an afternoon.

Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb.

The setup

The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script (bench.py):

  1. Measure the hardware and estimate theoretical ceilings before tuning.
  2. Change one variable at a time and bracket every candidate between two control runs (control → candidate → control). Keep a change only if it beats both controls without regressing other metrics.
  3. Log every run in PLAN.md, including regressions and dead ends.
  4. Pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks before declaring a winner.

bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled.

The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure:

  • HF Jobs for compute. The rtx-pro-6000 Job flavor uses the same GPU as the nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint ($2.75/h for both), so Job numbers transfer directly. A ~150-line driver (jobs/driver.py) takes a list of server configs, starts each one, runs an unmeasured warmup, calls bench.py unmodified, shuts the server down, and prints one ledger line per run. Because Jobs run on separate machines, the agent swept SGLang (lmsysorg/sglang:inkling-2-mini) and vLLM nightly (vllm/vllm-openai:nightly) in parallel.
  • CPU Jobs for reading engine source. When a flag was undocumented, the agent ran a cheap cpu-upgrade Job to grep the installed Python package inside the container. That is how it found SGLang's SGLANG_OPT_* environment variables and vLLM's speculative-config fields.
  • Inference Endpoints for deployment, created via hf endpoints deploy using the exact image digest and flags that passed verification.

The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding.

Results

Single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate.

Config (1× RTX PRO 6000) 1-user decode (tok/s) 8-user aggregate (tok/s) Prefill 4K / 32K (tok/s) TTFT
SGLang, no speculation (baseline) 134–139 543–598 18.7–19.1K / 16.9–19.1K 41–114 ms
vLLM, no speculation 157.0 638 20.7K / 20.7K 33 ms
SGLang + DSpark (8 drafts) 166.6 — ¹ 18.0–19.5K / 18.9–19.1K 38–51 ms
vLLM + DSpark (7 drafts) 190.6 716 20.7K / 20.6K 40 ms
Deployed endpoint (over the internet) 194.9 673 11.7K / 19.2K ² 198 ms ²

¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip.

All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB:

vllm serve thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini \
  --tool-call-parser inkling \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --reasoning-parser inkling \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'

Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work).

Why it stops around 190 tok/s

Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job (1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s. Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits.

Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s. At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth, so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer.

What didn't work

Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower:

vLLM

Lever Result
Shorter draft length (3–6) Rejected at startup; requires num_speculative_tokens = 7 (checkpoint block size − 1).
draft_sample_method: "greedy" −11% at temperature 1.0 (168.6 vs ~190.4 tok/s).
rejection_sample_method: "block" 190.1 vs 190.3–190.5 for controls; no effect.
enable_adaptive_verification Assertion error at startup for the Inkling 2 drafter.
draft_lm_head_quantization: "fp8" Only supported for DeepSeek DSpark drafters.

We also skipped rejection_sample_method: "fly" and "synthetic" on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup.

SGLang

Lever Result
Shorter draft length (3–6) Rejected at startup; requires --speculative-num-draft-tokens 8 (gamma + 1 for the bundled drafter).
SGLANG_ENABLE_NV_MEGA_RUNTIME_OPTIMIZATION=1 +4% once, failed to reproduce against fresh controls.
SGLANG_OPT_USE_FUSED_DRAFT_SAMPLE=1 +2%, within run-to-run noise.
SGLANG_OPT_MOE_QUANT_ONCE=1 +1%, within run-to-run noise.
SGLANG_DSPARK_USE_GREEDY_DRAFT=1 −9% at temperature 1.0 (156.8 vs ~172 tok/s).

Benchmarking gotchas

A few measurement issues caught us along the way:

  • Triton JIT during timed prefill. vLLM's first 4K prefill came back at 202 tok/s instead of 20K because Triton was compiling kernels during the timed request. Running an unmeasured warmup across prompt lengths and concurrency fixed 4K prefill, though the first run in each Job still under-reported 32K prefill due to last-chunk shape differences (flagged in the ledger).
  • Orphaned servers holding GPU memory. The initial driver stopped servers via a PID saved from setsid … &, which is not guaranteed to match the process group ID. The previous server stayed alive on port 8000, broke the next launch, and turned into a zombie that still passed kill -0. Managing the process with subprocess.Popen(start_new_session=True) and waiting until both GPU memory and port 8000 are free fixed it.
  • Hidden OOM errors in vLLM logs. vLLM + DSpark twice died with "Engine core initialization failed" at the end of the log while the real causes sat 200 lines up. First, the default 1M-token KV cache needed 52.6 GiB with only 48.1 GiB free alongside the drafter (--max-model-len 262144 fixed this). Next, because vLLM v0.34.0 raised the default --gpu-memory-utilization from 0.92 to 1.0, the KV cache claimed the remaining VRAM and OOMed the drafter's 5 GiB allocation (--gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 fixed this). The driver now prints every error line from the server log instead of just the tail.
  • Engine variance. Across identical runs with speculation, vLLM stayed within 0.4% while SGLang swung by ±4.5%. That was wide enough to make SGLANG_ENABLE_NV_MEGA_RUNTIME_OPTIMIZATION=1 look like a +4% win on its first run before repeat controls ruled it out.

Verification and deployment

Before deploying, we pinned the exact vLLM nightly digest (vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6…, build 0.34.0rc1.dev1235+gf2f9edcac) and ran the acceptance gates inside a Job:

Gate Result
Needle retrieval at ~50% context (126,537 tokens) 3/3, TTFT 12.5 s
Needle retrieval at ~95% context (249,970 tokens) 3/3, TTFT 28.7 s
Concurrent soak (4 × ~58K-token requests) 4/4 succeeded, 3/3 retrieval each
Greedy equivalence, DSpark vs no speculation (6 prompts, temp 0) 6/6 byte-identical
Single-user decode on pinned image 189.9 / 190.2 tok/s

Once those passed, we deployed the endpoint with a single hf endpoints deploy command, pinning both the image digest and model revision (authenticated access, scale-to-zero after 60 idle minutes):

hf endpoints deploy inkling2mini-tuned-dspark --namespace <your-org> \
  --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --revision 7a67ae2314b44ef05c87fd1d4d311c58aaeb18f6 \
  --framework custom --custom-image "vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6ee3aac77f3158e80ed79ec425db3a53f7cd666bf1954e96abfaf19a7" \
  --health-route /health --port 8000 \
  --vendor aws --region us-east-2 --accelerator gpu --instance-type nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 --instance-size x1 \
  --min-replica 0 --max-replica 1 --scale-to-zero-timeout 60 --type authenticated \
  --container-command "vllm serve" \
  --container-args "/repository --served-model-name thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --tool-call-parser inkling --enable-auto-tool-choice --reasoning-parser inkling --max-model-len 262144 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --speculative-config '{\"method\":\"dspark\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":7,\"draft_sample_method\":\"probabilistic\"}'"

Running bench.py against the live endpoint gave 194.9 tok/s single-user, matching the Job runs once network latency is accounted for.

Everything from this run (PLAN.md, THEORY.md, jobs/driver.py, submit.sh, deploy.sh, and the raw ledger-*.jsonl files) is in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb. To reuse the loop on another model, put your candidate and control server commands into a configs/plan-*.json file and submit it to whichever HF Jobs GPU flavor matches your target endpoint.
