Step 1. Define the claim


A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.
For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.
Domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.




Step 2. Find a starting task


For your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.




Step 3. Run the task unchanged


Before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.
We ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's hf-sandbox extra installed and HF_TOKEN set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.
harbor run -t terminal-bench/raman-fitting \
  -a oracle -e hf-sandbox

OPENAI_API_KEY="$HF_TOKEN" harbor run \
  -t terminal-bench/raman-fitting -k 3 -e hf-sandbox \
  -a terminus-2 -m openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b \
  --ak api_base=https://router.huggingface.co/v1

In these commands, -t names the task, -a the agent, -e the environment, -m the model, and -k the number of rollouts per task.
The model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.




Step 4. Adapt the task


We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.
The D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.
The original instruction.md shows why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.


Figure 6. The instruction.md files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the new parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.
The verifier is guided by three rules:
Grade what the agent produced: inspect the saved output, not its claim to have finished. τ-bench does this by comparing the final database state with an annotated goal state.
State every checked fact in the instruction, including units, parameter conventions, tolerances, and required fields.
Generate synthetic data from known parameters so the reference answer is available, then review whether the examples represent the intended problem.
The shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:
harbor task init my-org/task-01 -p datasets/my-evals





Step 5. Check the evaluation


Before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here datasets/my-evals contains the adapted tasks.
harbor run -p datasets/my-evals -a oracle -e hf-sandbox
harbor run -p datasets/my-evals -a nop -e hf-sandbox

The oracle should pass every task, i.e., the known solution must work in the supplied environment.
The no-op agent does nothing, so it should fail every task. A blank exam paper should not pass. A review of agentic benchmarks found one that counted empty responses as successes.
A shortcut that skips required work should fail. One way to test this is with a deliberately lazy solution, such as one that outputs a plausible answer without doing the work, to see whether the verifier accepts it. Also try plausible wrong answers and alternative correct methods, to catch both false passes and false failures.
Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.




Step 6. Run it and read the traces


It is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in agent/trajectory.json using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.
The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.


Figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called mark_task_complete in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.
Several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.
Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.
Finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.




Step 7. Report the score


The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:
pass@k asks whether at least one of k rollouts succeeds. Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once.
pass^k asks whether all k rollouts succeed. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time.
Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.
A mean is more useful with its uncertainty beside it. Rollouts of the same spectrum share its difficulty, so they are not independent, and the standard error should be clustered by task. Clustering gave a mean success rate of 0.46 with a standard error of about 0.11. A repeat run passed 10 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the first run. With only eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.
Harbor writes a result.json per rollout, which it calls a trial. We group these by task, check that each task has three rollouts, and record errors or exclusions. Reporting tokens, elapsed time, and tool calls beside the score lets readers compare setups that reach similar results at different costs.




Step 8. Compare models


When a single model fails a task, that run alone cannot tell us what went wrong. It could be the model, the agent harness, or the evaluation itself. Running more models on the same tasks helps narrow the possibilities. When several models fail the same task, inspect the instructions, environment, and verifier for a shared cause. When one model repeatedly fails in a distinctive way, compare its traces with successful attempts.
Inference Providers serves many open-weight models through the same router, so each new model is one more value for -m. Several providers can serve the same model with different quantization and context limits, so it helps to pin one with a suffix such as :deepinfra and record it beside the score.
OPENAI_API_KEY="$HF_TOKEN" harbor run -p datasets/my-evals -k 3 \
  -e hf-sandbox -a terminus-2 -m openai/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B:deepinfra \
  --ak api_base=https://router.huggingface.co/v1

Figure 8 shows the raman-lab results for each model.


Figure 8. raman-lab results per model, with pass@3, pass^3, and the mean pass rate with its clustered standard error. Select a square to inspect that rollout.
The comparison makes one pattern in gpt-oss-120b clearer: it often declares completion before seeing command output. In this separate run with DeepInfra pinned as the provider, it called mark_task_complete in its first response in 22 of 24 rollouts, while none of the other five models did so (Figure 9). The Step 6 run used the router's default provider and recorded 19 of 24 such early completions. It passed 11 of 24 rollouts, compared with 13 of 24 in the DeepInfra run. Both counts use the same test: whether the model called mark_task_complete in its first response.


Figure 9. raman-lab rollout outcomes by when the agent declared completion. Left: the agent observed command output first. Right: it called mark_task_complete in its first response.
The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.
Inference for all six models cost under $5 at the router's list prices. The median raman-lab rollout used about 6,000 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and about 90,000 for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. The companion repository holds the traces, the per-rollout results, and the scripts to add another model.




How we reused existing open components


Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. We could reuse them because Harbor and Terminal-Bench publish their code and tasks.
Task: We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. The new work was a narrower claim, skill coverage, and instructions for raman-lab.
Task data: The original spectrum served as a starting example. We built a generator for eight spectra with known parameters and reviewed them manually.
Environment: Harbor's environment support and HF Sandbox ran the tasks. We checked package requirements and diagnosed missing dependencies.
Agent harness and tools: Terminus-2 with shell access, with Inference Providers for model responses. This part needed no new work.
Rollout and trace: Harbor's rollout records and ATIF captured each run. We reviewed successes and failures and grouped them by cause.
Reference solution: We kept the convention of running solution/solve.sh and wrote a reference fit for each new task.
Evaluation harness: Harbor ran in an HF Job. We configured the run and grouped results by task.
Verifier: We reused the tests/test.sh entry point and its way of writing the score to a file. The new work was fit and ratio checks, plus tests for shortcuts and incorrect outputs.

Agent harness: The software around a model that turns its responses into actions, such as shell commands. Terminus-2 is the agent harness in this post.
Agentic evaluation: An evaluation that scores what an agent changed in an environment, not only the text it returned.
ATIF: Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, a shared format for recording an agent's messages, tool calls and observations.
Canary string: A unique marker in benchmark files that lets model trainers find and exclude them from training data.
Clustered standard error: A standard error that treats rollouts of the same task as related, which gives a wider and more honest margin than treating each rollout as independent.
Container image: A fixed package of operating system, files and software, so every rollout starts from the same environment.
Contamination: Test questions or solutions appearing in training data, so a score may reflect memory rather than skill.
Context limit: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.
D, G and 2D peaks: Features in graphene's Raman spectrum. G and 2D indicate the number of layers, and D appears when the carbon lattice has defects.
Defect ratio: The intensity of the D peak divided by that of the G peak, used to indicate defects in graphene. Also called the D-to-G ratio.
Development set: Tasks used while building and debugging an evaluation, as opposed to a held-back test set used for final scores.
Environment: The software, files and resources an agent works in during a task.
Evaluation harness: The software that runs tasks, repeats rollouts, collects traces and aggregates scores. Harbor is the evaluation harness in this post.
Gated dataset: A Hugging Face dataset that can be downloaded only after the owner approves an access request.
Harbor: An open-source evaluation harness for agentic tasks.
HF Job: Compute on Hugging Face that runs a script. Here it runs Harbor.
HF Sandbox: An isolated Hugging Face environment where a single rollout runs its commands and stores its files.
Held-out test set: Test items kept private so that models cannot be trained or tuned on them.
Inference Providers: A Hugging Face service that routes model requests to third-party providers through one API, called the router.
Lorentzian: A mathematical curve commonly used to model the shape of a spectral peak.
No-op agent: An agent that does nothing. A sound evaluation gives it a score of zero.
Open-weight model: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.
Oracle: An agent that runs the reference solution, used to check that every task can be solved in the supplied environment.
pass@k: The share of tasks where at least one of k rollouts succeeds.
pass^k: The share of tasks where all k rollouts succeed.
Pinning: Fixing the exact versions of software, images or model providers so a run can be repeated.
Quantization: Storing model weights at lower numerical precision to run faster and cheaper, which can change outputs slightly.
Raman shift: The difference in frequency between the laser light and the light a sample scatters, measured in cm⁻¹.
Raman spectroscopy: A technique that shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the scattered light to identify properties of the material.
Reference solution: A known correct way to complete a task, stored with the task.
Rollout: One attempt by an agent at one task. Harbor calls it a trial.
Run record: A record of what ran behind a score: the exact task, environment, model configuration and code versions.
Saturation: The point where most models reach top scores on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.
Synthetic data: Data generated from known parameters, so the correct answer is known in advance.
Terminal-Bench: An open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a computer terminal.
Terminus-2: The terminal agent harness used in this post. It connects the model to shell commands.
Token: The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.
Trace: The full record of a rollout: the model's messages, its tool calls and what each command returned. Also called a trajectory.
Verifier: The code that grades a rollout by checking the saved output or the environment's final state.

summaries.zh: 本文介绍了如何构建和维护代理式AI评估。评估设计经历了问答、代理和团队/群三个阶段，其中代理式评估因用户和企业的兴趣而日益重要。文章涵盖评估的四个方面：评估演变历程、代理式评估步骤、评估错误修正及开放策略。Hugging Face Hub作为AI评估中心，提供任务、环境和工具支持，促进开源共享以提升评估质量。代理式评估涉及任务指令、代理执行、环境交互等环节，需关注软件对评分的影响。
summaries.en: AI evaluations assess system performance through tasks and scoring, evolving into three eras: question-answering, agentic, and team/swarm benchmarks. Agentic evaluations, focused on agent actions and tool use within environments, are growing in prominence due to user interest in deployment. This guide outlines the anatomy of agentic evaluations, covering task definition, agent harnessing, and scoring, while emphasizing open-source sharing for transparency and improvement. It discusses evaluation design changes, common errors, and strategic openness of components. The Hugging Face hub hosts thousands of eval leaderboards and datasets, supporting agentic evaluation infrastructure.

items.title: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup
items.content:
Update on GitHub

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

What is new with Inkling 2 Mini?

Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.
The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

  • Each six-layer block has five sliding-window layers and one full-attention layer. The local window holds up to 1,024 tokens.
  • Attention uses 24 query heads and eight KV heads. It uses learned relative position logits, a learned sink, and an output gate. Full-attention layers use dynamic key and value convolutions.
  • The router selects eight of 128 SwiGLU experts for each token. It normalizes the selected scores and scales the weights by 8.
  • During passes 2 and 3, each core layer attends over two residual blocks from the previous pass. Four rank-64 gates mix separate messages into the query, key, value, and MoE inputs.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Benchmark Results

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

Inference Support

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

Transformers

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

Fixed loop with Inkling 2 Mini

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Why is the sky blue?"}]}]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)
print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))

Variable loop

To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research"

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    text_config={"loop_num_passes": 2},
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Why is the sky blue?"}]}]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, reasoning_effort="medium", tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt", 
).to(model.device)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)
print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))

Images and text

For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": "/path/to/image.jpg"},
            {"type": "text", "text": "What is in this image?"},
        ],
    }
]

Reasoning Effort

Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, reasoning_effort="medium", tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt", 
).to(model.device)

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

Tool calling

Let’s get our model to call some tools.

In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")


def get_current_temperature(location: str, unit: str):
    """
    Get the current temperature at a location.

    Args:
        location: The location to get the temperature for, in the format "City, Country"
        unit: The unit to return the temperature in. (choices: ["celsius", "fahrenheit"])
    """
    return 22.0  # A real function would call a weather API here


def ask(messages):
    inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
        messages, tools=[get_current_temperature], reasoning_effort="low", tokenize=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt"
    ).to(model.device)
    output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1] :]
    parsed = processor.parse_response(output, prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0])
    return parsed


messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Hey, what's the temperature in Paris right now?"}]

reply = ask(messages)
call = reply["tool_calls"][0]["function"]
print("Model calls:", call["name"], call["arguments"])  # the model fills in the arguments itself

temperature = get_current_temperature(**call["arguments"])
messages += [reply, {"role": "tool", "name": call["name"], "content": str(temperature)}]
print(ask(messages)["content"])

# Model calls: get_current_temperature {'location': 'Paris, France', 'unit': 'celsius'}
# Right now in Paris it’s about **22°C** (roughly **71.6°F**).

llama.cpp

The easiest way to run Inkling 2 locally is with the Llama App, available for macOS and Windows. After you have installed it on your computer, select your preferred GGUF quant on the Hub, click the "Use this model" button and select "Llama".

There are two quants you can use, the following links will trigger downloads from your Llama app if you have it installed:

  • IQ4_NL. Recommended for most users. The original nvfp4 weights are converted to a different 4-bit format, the mxfp8 ones are kept in fp8 precision. It fits in 32 GB of GPU RAM or unified memory.
  • Q8_0. Near lossless, but it requires more RAM and is slightly slower.

Example

Here we ask the 4-bit model to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. The model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic.

Command-line

If you are on Linux, or if you only want the command line, you can use the one-line installer:

curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh

For integration with other tools, you can launch a server compatible with the OpenAI API:

llama serve -hf ggml-org/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF:IQ4_NL

Change the suffix to :Q8_0 to load the 8-bit weights, or use the research model to experiment with a variable number of passes through the loop:

llama serve -hf ggml-org/TML-d24-varloop-research-GGUF:IQ4_NL

Integrations

Follow the docs to integrate your llama server with agents such as Pi, ChatGPT Desktop, and others.

SGLang

Inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.

export MODEL="thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path $MODEL \
  --served-model-name inkling \
  --attention-backend fa4 --bf16-gemm-backend torch --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tp 1 --page-size 128 --grammar-backend xgrammar \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

After the server is up you should be able to request the APIs like so

curl -s localhost:30000/health_generate && echo OK
curl -s localhost:30000/v1/models | python -m json.tool

curl -s localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "model": "inkling",
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 times 24?"}],
        "max_tokens": 512,
        "reasoning_effort": "low"
      }' | python -m json.tool

One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.

Speculative decoding

SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

Show SGLang benchmarking script 
MODEL=thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini

for TAG in base mtp; do
  EXTRA=""; [ $TAG = mtp ] && EXTRA="--speculative-algorithm DSPARK"

  # Start the server (with or without MTP)
  python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path $MODEL \
    --attention-backend fa4 --bf16-gemm-backend torch --dtype bfloat16 \
    --tp 1 --page-size 128 --context-length 131072 --max-running-requests 64 \
    --port 30000 $EXTRA > $TAG.log 2>&1 &
  until curl -sf localhost:30000/health_generate > /dev/null; do sleep 10; done

  # Benchmark at increasing concurrency
  for C in 1 4 16 64; do
    python -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --port 30000 --model $MODEL \
      --dataset-name random --apply-chat-template \
      --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 1024 --random-range-ratio 1.0 \
      --num-prompts $(( C*4 < 32 ? 32 : C*4 )) --max-concurrency $C \
      --output-file results_$TAG.jsonl
  done

  kill %1; wait
done

MLX

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

Here’s an example CLI invocation:

mlx_lm generate --model thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --image image.jpg --prompt "Describe this image.<|end_message|><|message_user|><|content_image|><|unused_200054|>" -m 1000

Demos and Vibe Tests

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

3D shader flythroughs

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

Sunset Ridge

Over the Still Sea

Show shared flythrough prompt

Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Starry Night, Alive

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889)

Inkling 2 Mini recreation

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

Show prompt

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

Napkin to App

Input napkin sketch

Generated Trip Split app

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

Show prompt

The photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

4-bit Model

We ask the 4-bit GGUF quantized Inkling 2 Mini (IQ4_NL) to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists.

Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”.

“Make yourself into a browser agent"

We have paired Inkling 2 Mini with Pi coding agent to build itself into a browser agent using Helium, Chromium and Hugging Face Sandboxes. We provide the traces and the final file (that can be used as a browser agent) in this bucket.

Wrapping Up

We are very glad to partner with Thinking Machines Lab to ship Inkling 2 Mini, a performant mid-sized model for local setups. Give this model a try and let us know what you think in comments!

The router selects eight of 128 SwiGLU experts for each token. It normalizes the selected scores and scales the weights by 8.  
During passes 2 and 3, each core layer attends over two residual blocks from the previous pass. Four rank-64 gates mix separate messages into the query, key, value, and MoE inputs.
Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.
In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.




Benchmark Results


Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.
Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.





Inference Support


In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.




Transformers


We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.




Fixed loop with Inkling 2 Mini


You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Why is the sky blue?"}]}]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)
print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))





Variable loop


To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research"

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    text_config={"loop_num_passes": 2},
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Why is the sky blue?"}]}]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, reasoning_effort="medium", tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt", 
).to(model.device)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)
print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))





Images and text


For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.
messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": "/path/to/image.jpg"},
            {"type": "text", "text": "What is in this image?"},
        ],
    }
]





Reasoning Effort


Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, reasoning_effort="medium", tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt", 
).to(model.device)

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.




Tool calling


Let’s get our model to call some tools.
In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.
If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")


def get_current_temperature(location: str, unit: str):
    """
    Get the current temperature at a location.

    Args:
        location: The location to get the temperature for, in the format "City, Country"
        unit: The unit to return the temperature in. (choices: ["celsius", "fahrenheit"])
    """
    return 22.0  # A real function would call a weather API here


def ask(messages):
    inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
        messages, tools=[get_current_temperature], reasoning_effort="low", tokenize=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt"
    ).to(model.device)
    output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1] :]
    parsed = processor.parse_response(output, prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0])
    return parsed


messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Hey, what's the temperature in Paris right now?"}]

reply = ask(messages)
call = reply["tool_calls"][0]["function"]
print("Model calls:", call["name"], call["arguments"])  # the model fills in the arguments itself

temperature = get_current_temperature(**call["arguments"])
messages += [reply, {"role": "tool", "name": call["name"], "content": str(temperature)}]
print(ask(messages)["content"])

# Model calls: get_current_temperature {'location': 'Paris, France', 'unit': 'celsius'}
# Right now in Paris it’s about **22°C** (roughly **71.6°F**).





llama.cpp


The easiest way to run Inkling 2 locally is with the Llama App, available for macOS and Windows. After you have installed it on your computer, select your preferred GGUF quant on the Hub, click the "Use this model" button and select "Llama".

There are two quants you can use, the following links will trigger downloads from your Llama app if you have it installed:
IQ4_NL. Recommended for most users. The original nvfp4 weights are converted to a different 4-bit format, the mxfp8 ones are kept in fp8 precision. It fits in 32 GB of GPU RAM or unified memory.
Q8_0. Near lossless, but it requires more RAM and is slightly slower.
Example
Here we ask the 4-bit model to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. The model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic.

Command-line
If you are on Linux, or if you only want the command line, you can use the one-line installer:
curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh

For integration with other tools, you can launch a server compatible with the OpenAI API:
llama serve -hf ggml-org/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF:IQ4_NL

Change the suffix to :Q8_0 to load the 8-bit weights, or use the research model to experiment with a variable number of passes through the loop:
llama serve -hf ggml-org/TML-d24-varloop-research-GGUF:IQ4_NL

Integrations
Follow the docs to integrate your llama server with agents such as Pi, ChatGPT Desktop, and others.




SGLang


Inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.
export MODEL="thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path $MODEL \
  --served-model-name inkling \
  --attention-backend fa4 --bf16-gemm-backend torch --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tp 1 --page-size 128 --grammar-backend xgrammar \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

After the server is up you should be able to request the APIs like so
curl -s localhost:30000/health_generate && echo OK
curl -s localhost:30000/v1/models | python -m json.tool

curl -s localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "model": "inkling",
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 times 24?"}],
        "max_tokens": 512,
        "reasoning_effort": "low"
      }' | python -m json.tool

One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.




Speculative decoding


SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.
We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.
Show SGLang benchmarking script

MODEL=thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini

for TAG in base mtp; do
  EXTRA=""; [ $TAG = mtp ] && EXTRA="--speculative-algorithm DSPARK"

  # Start the server (with or without MTP)
  python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path $MODEL \
    --attention-backend fa4 --bf16-gemm-backend torch --dtype bfloat16 \
    --tp 1 --page-size 128 --context-length 131072 --max-running-requests 64 \
    --port 30000 $EXTRA > $TAG.log 2>&1 &
  until curl -sf localhost:30000/health_generate > /dev/null; do sleep 10; done

  # Benchmark at increasing concurrency
  for C in 1 4 16 64; do
    python -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --port 30000 --model $MODEL \
      --dataset-name random --apply-chat-template \
      --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 1024 --random-range-ratio 1.0 \
      --num-prompts $(( C*4 < 32 ? 32 : C*4 )) --max-concurrency $C \
      --output-file results_$TAG.jsonl
  done

  kill %1; wait
done






MLX


We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.
MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.
Here’s an example CLI invocation:
mlx_lm generate --model thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --image image.jpg --prompt "Describe this image.<|end_message|><|message_user|><|content_image|><|unused_200054|>" -m 1000





Demos and Vibe Tests


We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.




3D shader flythroughs


The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.
Sunset Ridge

Over the Still Sea

Show shared flythrough prompt

Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.









Starry Night, Alive



  
Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889)

    
Inkling 2 Mini recreation
We gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.
Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.
Show prompt

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.









Napkin to App



  

    
Input napkin sketch

    
Generated Trip Split app
We gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.
We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.
Show prompt

The photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.









4-bit Model


We ask the 4-bit GGUF quantized Inkling 2 Mini (IQ4_NL) to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. 
Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”. 





“Make yourself into a browser agent"


We have paired Inkling 2 Mini with Pi coding agent to build itself into a browser agent using Helium, Chromium and Hugging Face Sandboxes. We provide the traces and the final file (that can be used as a browser agent) in this bucket. 




Wrapping Up


We are very glad to partner with Thinking Machines Lab to ship Inkling 2 Mini, a performant mid-sized model for local setups. Give this model a try and let us know what you think in comments!

summaries.zh: Inkling 2 Mini 是一款新型循环 Transformer 模型，采用多模态专家混合架构，总参数量约 26B，每 token 活跃参数 3B。通过循环重复部分层（12 层重复 3 次）来提升模型容量，支持 1M-Token 上下文，可接受图像和文本输入。该模型专为本地 AI 部署设计，性能与 Qwen 3.8 27B 相当，支持 transformers、llama.cpp 和 MLX 等框架。此外，还提供可变循环版本以加速推理。在 AAv5 等基准测试中表现优异，尤其在编码、推理等领域领先。
summaries.en: Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model with ~26B parameters and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a looped architecture where 12 middle layers run three times, effectively acting as a 48-layer model with 24 physical layers. The model supports multimodal inputs (text and images) and a 1M-token context size. It delivers cutting-edge performance for local setups, comparable to Qwen 3.8 27B in vibe tests. The model includes a DSpark drafter for speed-up and supports transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang. It outperforms competitors in 32 out of 48 benchmarks across coding, reasoning, and vision tasks. A variable-loop research variant is also available for faster inference at slightly lower quality.
